children.text: This is the Miniloc Island lagoon complex at the heart of El Nido's Tour A. In a single day you can kayak into Big Lagoon, ringed by limestone cliffs, and then reach Secret Lagoon, which appears only after you pass through a hole in the rock — which is why it is the spot most often recommended to first-time visitors to El Nido.
Miniloc Island is a limestone island about
20–40 minutes

by boat from El Nido town, deep inside Bacuit Bay. The cliffs around it rise straight out of the water, so most of the shoreline has no sand to land on, and tucked inside those cliffs are Big Lagoon, Secret Lagoon and Small Lagoon. This guide concentrates on the two highlights of Tour A: Big Lagoon and Secret Lagoon.

Big Lagoon is a half-enclosed lagoon with cliffs on every side, and it is the largest of the three. The boat drops anchor outside the entrance, and visitors either paddle a kayak or swim in through the shallow entrance channel. Once inside, the water shifts from jade to deep turquoise and the black cliffs rise straight to the sky in a single frame; no engine noise reaches in, so all you hear is the dip of paddles. The water is said to be shallow near the entrance and a few meters deep farther in.
Secret Lagoon lies on the southwest coast of the same island, roughly
1.5km

in a straight line from Big Lagoon by the coordinates. As the name suggests, it cannot be seen from outside: you pass through a small hole in a rock wall and a round, pool-like lagoon opens up. Because the cliffs shade it all day the water is cool, and only a few people can go in at a time, so you may have to wait your turn. It is a different place from Small Lagoon, also on Tour A, and from Secret Beach on Tour C, so double-check the names when you book.

Both lagoons lie inside the El Nido-Taytay Managed Resource Protected Area and require the El Nido municipal environmental fee; they cannot be reached on foot or by road, and a bangka boat is the only way in. Basic swimming ability and a life jacket are assumed, and because the Secret Lagoon entrance means climbing onto rock and ducking low, it can be hard for small children or anyone with limited mobility. Still, for travelers who want the essence of El Nido's lagoons in one go, and for couples or friends who love photos and kayaking, this is the first route to recommend. For the wider trip plan, see
El Nido
as well.

Switching from the boat anchored outside to a kayak and paddling through the channel between the cliffs is the heart of the experience here. The kayak rental is often charged separately, so check whether it is included when you book the tour.

Even without a kayak, you can put on a life jacket and swim from the boat into the shallow entrance channel. The water is clear enough to see the bottom, and the cliffs look most imposing when you look up at them from the entrance.

blocks.title: Floating in the middle of Big Lagoon

children.text: Paddle all the way to the inner part of the lagoon, then stop the kayak and just float on the water. The light reflected off the cliffs and spreading across the surface looks best in the morning sun. Snorkeling here is light at best; this is not a place to expect coral views.

blocks.title: Passing through the Secret Lagoon hole

children.text: Duck or crawl through the small hole in the rock wall and the round lagoon opens up before you. The entrance changes with the tide: some days you walk in, other days you wade through chest-deep water.

The sky opens in a circle and cliffs surround you on all sides, giving photos a completely different feel from the other lagoons. Visitors usually stay about 30 minutes, and boatmen warn that the water gets deeper the farther in you go.

blocks.title: Resting on the sand outside the entrance

children.text: Below the cliff in front of the Secret Lagoon entrance there is a small sandy shore where bangka boats nose up and anchor. It is a good place to wait your turn in the shade of the palms or to dip your feet in the water.

blocks.title: A route that includes Small Lagoon

children.text: Tour A often visits Small Lagoon on the same island as well. You can compare the large Big Lagoon, the compact Small Lagoon and the hidden Secret Lagoon in a single day, which sums up the appeal of Miniloc in one go.

blocks.title: Starting early for a quieter visit

children.text: If you reach Big Lagoon in the early morning, before the boats crowd in, the kayaks are spread out and it feels peaceful. Simply asking the operator to visit "Big Lagoon first" changes the quality of your photos a great deal.

A private boat lets you set the order of stops yourself, so you can choose the times when the popular lagoons are quiet. Prices differ a lot by boat size and operator, so get quotes from several places.
To reach Miniloc Island you first have to get to
El Nido
. A shared van from Puerto Princesa airport takes about
5–6 hours
and costs about
, and a fast ferry from Coron takes about
3 hours 30 minutes–4 hours
. Direct flight arrangements from Manila have changed recently, so check the airline's latest announcements.
You reach Big Lagoon and Secret Lagoon on the Tour A boat that leaves from El Nido town or Corong-Corong Beach. It usually departs at
, the trip to the island takes about
20–40 minutes
, and depending on the order Big Lagoon may not be the first stop. Many operators offer free pickup from your hotel to the tour office or the pier.
A shared tour leaves once the boat fills up, and includes lunch, life jackets and snorkeling gear.
The environmental fee and lagoon entrance fee are often paid separately, depending on the operator.
You can book at a tour office, through your accommodation or online, but the tour can be canceled on days with bad sea weather.

If your group is four to six people, renting a whole bangka boat lets you set the order of stops yourself, and the cost per person is reasonable. Agree in advance on the time at each lagoon and the lunch spot, and you can also ask them to schedule Secret Lagoon for a time when the tide is low.

If you stay at the luxury resort on Miniloc Island, the resort's own boat takes you from the island to the lagoons. You can see the quiet lagoons earlier than the regular tours do, but room rates are much higher, so choose according to your budget and schedule.
The dry season from
December
to
May
is best for Big Lagoon and Secret Lagoon.
December–February
has clear underwater visibility and cool weather, and in
March–May
the sea is calm, which makes kayaking and passing through Secret Lagoon easier. However,
March–May
also coincides with Holy Week and school holidays, when boats crowd the lagoons. From
June
to
October
the southwest monsoon brings high waves, so tours are sometimes canceled or rerouted, and in
October–November
typhoons may pass through.
During the day, boats start to crowd in after
10 AM

and it is busiest around noon, so arriving early pays off. The height of the Secret Lagoon entrance changes with the tide, so how hard it is to get through differs greatly by time of day even on the same day; ask your boatman about today's tide before you leave.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary with local conditions.
The boats to Big Lagoon and Secret Lagoon mostly leave from El Nido town or Corong-Corong Beach, so staying in town (Poblacion) or around Corong-Corong is the easiest. Guesthouses cost about
a night and mid-range hotels about

. It is easy to ask for an early departure the day before, and some places can arrange pickup from the hotel to the pier. On Miniloc Island itself there is a luxury resort that takes up a whole island, and its guests have the advantage of seeing the quiet lagoons earlier than the regular tours.

Tour lunch is typically grilled fish and pork barbecue cooked by the boatmen on the boat or on a beach, with rice and fresh fruit. There is nowhere to buy food at the lagoons, so bring plenty of snacks and water. In the evening after the tour, choosing the day's catch and ordering it by weight at a beachfront restaurant in town is popular, and a meal budget is about
each.
The environmental fee is often accepted in cash only, and the receipt is usually checked during the tour. Keep the receipt in a waterproof pouch.
If you ask when booking for an order that reaches Big Lagoon before
, it will be at its quietest. Around noon, ten or more boats may gather there.
Water shoes are essential. It is easy to hurt your feet on the rocks at the Secret Lagoon entrance and on the coral in shallow water.
Bring a dry bag or waterproof case. In the entrance channel the kayak can wobble and splash, which easily soaks electronics.
Use reef-safe sunscreen, and apply it before you get in so it does not wash into the water.
Most kayaks are two-seaters, so it helps to split roles: one person steers from the front while the other helps paddle.
Before entering Secret Lagoon, ask your boatman about the tide and waves, and if they say it is not safe, it is better not to go in.
Tour routes change with the weather and tide, so if there is a lagoon you particularly want to see, confirm "Big Lagoon entrance guaranteed" when you book.

The Secret Lagoon entrance has sharp rocks, and depending on the tide the water can be deep enough that you get hurt or cannot enter. On days with high waves, and at high tide when it is unsafe, follow your boatman's judgment.
Keep your life jacket on in the lagoons, and if you are a weak swimmer do not go into deep water.
Standing on or touching coral and rocks is not allowed, and you must not leave trash or single-use plastic behind.
Rules, fees and visitor limits change often according to notices from the municipal tourism office and the protected-area office, so check the latest announcements.
Tours sold by unlicensed touts may skip entrance fees or the environmental fee, or change the route, so use a licensed operator.
The midday sun is strong, and sunburn and dehydration are common. Bring a rash guard and plenty of water.
